blocks.heading: The season of tefillah and Moshe's prayers

paragraphs.text: The Rav opens by saying that this week's parsha teaches about tefillah, at the time when the work toward Rosh Hashanah begins, a season of prayer that stretches until Shemini Atzeres. The Beis Hamikdash, which the passuk in Yeshayahu calls a house of prayer, is at the center of this season.

Moshe Rabbeinu pleaded with many prayers to enter the land and see 'the good mountain and the Levanon', which the Rav reads as the Beis Hamikdash. In place of the Beis Hamikdash we now have tefillah, and Moshe teaches in this parsha how to daven.

blocks.heading: Three stages of davening: cutting a path

paragraphs.text: The Rav distinguishes three prayers named in Tehillim: the 'prayer of Moshe', a tefillah of contemplation on the greatness of Hashem; the 'prayer of the poor man'; and the prayer of David, the songs of Tehillim of the sweet singer of Israel. Davening likewise has three stages: korbanos, pesukei dezimra, and then the contemplative tefillah.

He explains the order with a parable. An army that wants to reach a place held by the enemy first fires into the enemy's positions and then cuts its way through. The air is full of forces born of sins that block tefillah; the korbanos, whose fragrance rises, drive them off, and pesukei dezimra, from zemer, to cut, cut through. David, who fought the wars of Hashem, cuts the path with his songs, just as the shofar does on Rosh Hashanah.

This is the lesson Chazal learn from Moshe here: first set out the praise of Hashem, honoring the King, and only then ask. The korbanos and pesukei dezimra prepare the heart so that the mind can open for contemplation.

blocks.heading: Why pesukei dezimra is not taken lightly

paragraphs.text: The Rav laments that many, even bnei Torah who know the halachos, treat pesukei dezimra lightly because it is less binding than the blessings of Shema, and skip it. He answers that the dearer a thing is, the less it is an obligation: bread one must provide, but a gift beyond that is worth more. The blessings of Shema were set by the Anshei Knesses Hagedolah; pesukei dezimra come from David Hamelech himself.

blocks.heading: Hiddur and Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair

paragraphs.text: He adds that the hiddur of a mitzvah gives Hashem more pleasure than the mitzvah itself. He brings the Gemara about Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair and the river Ginai: the river was doing a certain mitzvah and he only a doubtful one, yet he prevailed, because self-sacrifice for a doubtful mitzvah shows greater devotion. So, the Rav concludes, one who wants only his obligation relies on the blessings of Shema; one who wants what is dear to Hashem says David's chapters.

blocks.heading: Singing together; Shabbos and Hallel Hagadol

paragraphs.text: Old siddurim, the Rav notes, mark Baruch She'amar so that everyone says it together, not one here and another there, just as the angels sing in unison. On Shabbos many more chapters are added, because Shabbos lifts all the tefillos of the week, and the tzaddikim said great things about Hallel Hagadol and Nishmas.

In Hallel Hagadol, with its refrain 'ki l'olam chasdo', each angel is limited to a single praise, one for the luminaries, another for something else. A Jew who says them all includes the whole row of angels.

Earlier generations waited all week to say Nishmas and cried it out together, because there one receives the extra soul of Shabbos day. The Rav cites the Arizal that even one who received it Friday night receives it again in the morning.

He tells how Rebbe Moshe Leib of Sassov, on a mission of pidyon shvuyim at a poritz's lavish feast, was so hungry he feared fainting. He thought that Shabbos would soon come and he would say Nishmas, and its sweetness made him forget his hunger.

blocks.heading: Shabbos is all song; Moshe in every shul

paragraphs.text: On weekdays the alphabetic blessing before Shema has a word for each letter; on Shabbos 'Kel Adon' has a whole phrase for each letter, because Shabbos's added holiness is all song. The Rav urges davening together near the shliach tzibbur, and says that when the parsha is read Moshe Rabbeinu comes to every shul to teach how to daven in this season.

blocks.heading: Davening with the tzibbur, on time

paragraphs.text: The Rav asks that people come on time and daven together, like a full orchestra, as in the closing psalm of Tehillim with its instruments and 'let every soul praise'. One should keep pace with the chazzan and not lag behind.

The later Shabbos davening of chassidim, he explains, did not come from sleeping late. People busy all week used Shabbos morning to learn before davening and came to tefillah prepared and warmed; using the custom as a reason to sleep late was never its intent.

blocks.heading: What one owes the tzibbur; Torah with tefillah

paragraphs.text: Each person, the Rav says, is part of the congregation and owes it something: to come early, keep pace with the chazzan, and daven with life so as to arouse others. One who does not, withholds what he owes the tzibbur.

Shabbos is a day of Torah for those who work all week, and Torah and tefillah need each other. As the nights grow longer one must strengthen one's learning in preparation for the holy days ahead, and this Shabbos is a time to take on more in Torah and in tefillah. He asks what brings the redemption closer, and answers: learning Torah and tefillah.

blocks.heading: Why a Jew comes to a place

paragraphs.text: Every step of a person, the Rav teaches, is decreed above. His soul is not contained in his body but scattered, and he is led to places to gather its parts and redeem souls found there; each day he should consider why he was brought there.

A chassid of the Rebbe Reb Elimelech, lost and near death from thirst, found a stream, held back, and made a shehakol with great kavanah, then a borei nefashos. The Rebbe later said souls had been trapped there for centuries and the chassid's two blessings freed them.
So in camp one should ask why he was sent, use every minute, and stay united; Korach, the man of strife, stood against the unity of Klal Yisrael.

The Rav tells a story he heard in Eretz Yisrael. A simple melamed, hired for a season by a farmer, saw something wrong in the farmer's house and decided he must go to the Rebbe Reb Elimelech. At winter's end, through deep mud and in torn shoes, he ran with all his strength, and there was great joy in heaven over his self-sacrifice.

The Satan, who could not let such self-sacrifice pass, disguised himself as the melamed's uncle and met him on the road. He berated him as a fool who had a job and should mind his own business, until he talked him into turning back. The Rebbe Reb Elimelech told this to a young man who was thinking of no longer coming to his minyan, and said: the same uncle is here.

The same uncle, the Rav says, still comes in many forms whenever a Jew undertakes something good, arguing that it does not pay; one must identify him. Robbers do not ambush a garbage truck, only the truck carrying the bank's money.

He stresses peace among the boys: no vessel holds blessing but peace, and Hashem blesses His people with peace. The very first siman of Shulchan Aruch teaches not to be ashamed before those who mock; one needs a holy boldness, as when one sits learning while others play ball.

blocks.heading: Toil in tefillah and davening aloud

paragraphs.text: Tefillah needs toil just as Torah does. Chazal call it the service of the heart, and one who moves his lips for half an hour without his heart has not truly davened. One must daven alive, with warmth, not like a dead cat.

On davening in a raised voice, the Rav cites the Tanya that it awakens hislahavus. Views differ, each by the root of his soul, but our coarse bodies need the fire of hislahavus to break through as through an iron wall. Praise, unlike requests, is said aloud, as the angels in Yechezkel say their praise with a great noise.

blocks.heading: The first thought; use every minute

paragraphs.text: When a person wakes early and thinks to get up and learn, then a second thought argues him back, the first message comes from the soul; the second is a reaction of imagination.

The Rav closes by urging the boys to use every minute in camp, where one can gain more yiras shamayim than in a whole year: opening a Gemara, a kapitel Tehillim, a good word to a friend. He ends with a brachah.
